title: Chronic exposure to a natural deoxygenation gradient underpins membrane and energy storage lipid restructuring in a benthic marine invertebrate
content:
Abstract

Lipids are central to animal physiology, underpinning energy storage, membrane architecture, and cell signaling. Targeted lipid studies in wild animals have already demonstrated that lipid adjustments, such as shifts in energy storage and membrane composition, are key molecular responses to environmental stressors. Yet, in situ lipidome-wide responses remain virtually unexplored in marine invertebrates, particularly in systems affected by chronic environmental deoxygenation. Here, we characterized for the first time the whole-body lipidome of the benthic marine annelid Neoleanira tetragona collected from sites across a naturally occurring deoxygenation gradient, with over 1700 lipids identified and quantified via untargeted high-resolution lipidomics. Individuals from less oxygenated areas exhibited an enrichment in triacylglycerols, indicating increased lipid storage, and membrane lipids with lower fatty acid unsaturation. In contrast, an enrichment of acylcarnitines in individuals from more oxygenated areas suggests increased lipid catabolism and turnover. We interpret these findings as a display of moderate capacity for lipidome-wide remodeling under chronic deoxygenation. We propose that this remodeling is due to physiological trade-offs between energy conservation, cellular protection and membrane architecture. Finally, by applying a breakpoint analysis we identify a potential molecular tipping point of O2 availability (~ 56.6 ± 8.7 μM), providing a first step toward mechanistically explaining a previously identified biogeochemical and community-level tipping point (~ 63 μM) to environmental change. Our work demonstrates that lipid-wide remodeling represents a chronic physiological response to deoxygenation, detected in situ, offering a link between biochemical and community-level tipping points in a naturally exposed marine invertebrate.
